clue.text: Prospect of snarl-up at start of White Queen's rule

definitions.meaning: a traffic jam that lies ahead, one due on the following day
in Through the Looking-Glass the White Queen offers jam every other day, the rule being jam yesterday and jam in the future but never jam today

explanation.surface: Someone foresees traffic chaos at the outset of a fairy-tale monarch's reign.
explanation.walkthrough: The White Queen is from Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass; the phrase has come to mean a promised treat that never arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: A snarl-up is a traffic jam, and a jam due the next day is a prospect; the Carroll rule gives the idiom for pleasures endlessly deferred.

clue.text: Manoeuvres to provide hip replacements?

definitions.meaning: military manoeuvres carried out by combined forces
read whimsically as surgery on the joints of the body, the hip being a joint

explanation.surface: Someone wonders which manoeuvres are needed to supply new hips.
explanation.definitionFit: Combined-service military actions are called by this name, a standard term for manoeuvres; the second reading treats it as surgery on joints.

clue.text: Gets tied up for months with soldiers on board

indicators.note: something on board is carried inside, so the soldiers sit within the months

parts.note: MOS is short for months
OR stands for Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Something is delayed for months while troops are carried aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets tied up' sounds like being delayed, but it means fastening a boat at a mooring.
explanation.definitionFit: To moor a vessel is to tie it up at a berth, so a boat that does this gets tied up.

clue.text: Towards the land of the unsettled hero son

indicators.note: unsettled describes the letters of these two words being stirred out of their order

explanation.surface: A heroic son with an unsettled nature heads for the shore.
explanation.definitionFit: Onshore means moving or directed towards the land from the sea, as an onshore wind does.

clue.text: Genteel interruption of poem about clergyman getting up late

indicators.note: the poem wraps around the clergyman, holding his letters within it
an interruption breaks into the middle, so the genteel letter goes inside the poem

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
U means upper-class or genteel, from the old U and non-U distinction

indicators.note: in a down clue getting up means the clergyman's abbreviation is read upwards, back to front

parts.note: Rev is short for Reverend, a clergyman

explanation.surface: A refined person interrupts a poem about a vicar who rose late.
explanation.walkthrough: Two insertions happen: 'interruption of' puts U inside the poem, and 'getting up' turns the clergyman so VER sits after the opening O, with 'about' signalling the poem holds him.
explanation.definitionFit: Something overdue has passed the time it was expected, so it is late.

clue.text: Knock a big town's greed

parts.note: a rap is a sharp knock
a city is a big town

explanation.surface: A rebuke of a large town's greed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock' looks like criticism of the town, but it gives RAP as a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapacity is grasping greed, an aggressive wish to seize what others have.

clue.text: Favourites of the Olympians?

parts.note: the Olympians are the gods of Mount Olympus, and those they favour, in the old saying, die young

explanation.surface: Who are the darlings of the Greek gods?
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from the proverb that those loved by the gods die young; 'Olympians' may suggest athletes, but here they are the gods.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names those the deities hold dear, and the Olympians were the Greek deities living on Mount Olympus.

clue.text: Battle of words, the Lib version

indicators.note: a version is a rendering in another form, so these letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A political war of words in the Liberal party's telling.
explanation.walkthrough: BOSWORTH FIELD was the 1485 battle in which Richard III was killed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bosworth Field was the decisive 1485 English battle ending the Wars of the Roses.

clue.text: A heavyweight, Elsie's out on the river taking it easy

parts.note: a ton is a heavy weight

indicators.note: out means the name and its ending are jumbled into a different order

parts.note: the name with its possessive ending supplies the letters as written
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A heavy Elsie lounges by the riverside, relaxing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' turns ELSIES into ESLEIS; 'on the' is a link placing the river last.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something at one's leisure is to do it without hurry, which is taking it easy.

clue.text: Portentous mantra intoned by one with common sense

parts.note: om is the sacred syllable chanted as a mantra
I is the Roman numeral one
nous is British slang for common sense

explanation.surface: A sage with good sense chants a weighty mantra.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ominous is threatening, giving a portent of trouble to come, so it is portentous.

clue.text: Previous story line includes one great deed

parts.note: ex means former or previous, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: includes means the story line holds the numeral within it

parts.note: a plot is the line of a story
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An earlier narrative thread contains a heroic act.
explanation.definitionFit: An exploit is a bold or daring feat, a great deed.

clue.text: Braved this awful time in the forest

indicators.note: in places the jumbled word and the time inside the forest

parts.note: a wood is a forest

indicators.note: awful suggests the word this is mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone endured a dreadful spell lost among the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges the four-letter word to give ITHS, which joins the time letter inside the forest; 'Braved' is the past tense, matching the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To have withstood something is to have resisted or faced it, which is having braved it.

clue.text: Copper can interpose

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a tin is a can

explanation.surface: A police officer is able to step in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' reads as a policeman and 'can' as 'is able', but they are the metal and a container.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut in is to interrupt or push in, so it means to interpose.

clue.text: Russian leader liable to be wholly engrossed

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: apt means liable or likely to

explanation.surface: A Kremlin chief is apt to be completely absorbed.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapt means completely absorbed, so wholly engrossed in something.

clue.text: Fast man entering small residence, becoming cruel

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so the fast and the man go into the residence

parts.note: res is the short form of residence
Lent is the Christian season of fasting
Les is a man's name

explanation.surface: A quick fellow barges into a little home and turns nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' reads as speedy, but it is the period of fasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Relentless means unyielding and pitiless, close to cruel.

clue.text: Remote participation of a defaulter I organised

indicators.note: the answer takes part in these words, its letters running across them

explanation.surface: A defaulter I organised has some distant involvement.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulterior can mean lying beyond or more remote, as well as hidden.

clue.text: Desultory help about painting the bog over in Geordieland

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go around the painting
desultory means random, so the letters of help are set in no particular order

parts.note: art covers painting

indicators.note: over means the bog is turned back to front

parts.note: bog is British slang for a toilet, the loo

explanation.surface: Random help with a painting of the toilet up in Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desultory' gives HLEP, split after its H to hold the painting; 'over' turns the toilet word into OOL. Hartlepool is a town in north-east England, near Geordie country.
explanation.definitionFit: Hartlepool is a port town in north-east England, the region whose people are loosely called Geordies.

clue.text: Go back after parking to take the lead

indicators.note: after places the going back behind the parking letter

parts.note: to recede is to go back

explanation.surface: Reverse out of a parking space to get ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: To precede is to go before, which is to take the lead.

clue.text: Keys for beginners

definitions.meaning: things that open locks or tins
those who start things off, such as batsmen who start an innings

explanation.surface: Introductory keyboard lessons for novices.
explanation.definitionFit: Openers are tools for opening, like keys, and also people or items that begin something.

clue.text: Manage to turn back time, not hard

indicators.note: not means the letter for hard is dropped
turn back means the word for time is read backwards

parts.note: an epoch is a period of time
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Trying to reverse the clock without difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: EPOCH turned round is HCOPE; dropping the H leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To cope is to manage or get by in a difficult situation.

clue.text: Fibre leads to incontinence, say the latest experts

indicators.note: the leads of the words are their first letters, taken in order

explanation.surface: Experts claim a fibre-rich diet helps with incontinence.
explanation.definitionFit: Istle is a plant fibre from agave and yucca, used for cordage and brushes.

clue.text: Poor egghead Eric's sex regime can be exhausting

parts.note: the head of egg is its first letter, E

indicators.note: poor suggests these letters are in bad shape and must be rearranged

parts.note: these words supply their letters as written

explanation.surface: A frail intellectual's sexual routine wears him out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be exhausting' is the surface's flourish, linking the regime to the effort it takes.
explanation.definitionFit: A training regime is made up of physical drills, so the plural noun describes such a programme.

clue.text: Derrick hurried into church

indicators.note: into means the hurrying goes inside the church

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
ran means hurried

explanation.surface: Someone named Derrick rushed into a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Derrick' looks like a man's name, but a derrick is a lifting machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A derrick is a kind of hoisting machine for lifting heavy loads, as a crane is.

clue.text: One over the eight following the sign of the beast

indicators.note: following puts the number after the sign

parts.note: Leo is a zodiac sign, the lion
one more than eight is nine; the phrase also means a drink too many

explanation.surface: A drink too many after a sign of the Beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for slightly drunk, but here it is literal arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonine means lion-like, belonging to the king of beasts.

clue.text: Woman doctor's game about to take one's fancy

parts.note: Ena is a woman's name
MO is a medical officer, a doctor

indicators.note: about means the game's letters are reversed

parts.note: RU stands for rugby union

explanation.surface: A female doctor's sport is about to catch someone's eye.
explanation.definitionFit: To enamour is to charm or captivate, so to take someone's fancy.

clue.text: Pedestrian bit of drama?

parts.note: pedestrian suggests dull, but here it means people on foot in a road setting, staged as a play

explanation.surface: A dull extract from a stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: Street Scene is a 1929 play by Elmer Rice, later an opera by Kurt Weill.
explanation.definitionFit: A depiction of life on a public road suits pedestrians, and it is also the title of a well-known play.
